Who bills Philadelphia property tax and where can I pay?

The Department of Revenue bills and collects the Real Estate Tax in Philadelphia, and the Office of Property Assessment supplies the value it is based on. Owners pay once a year, with a single March 31 due date covering both the City and the School District.

  • Online: the Philadelphia Tax Center, using the property address or the OPA account number. An eCheck carries no processing charge, while debit and credit cards do.
  • By phone: (833) 913-0795.
  • By mail: check or money order payable to the City of Philadelphia, sent with the OPA account number to Department of Revenue, PO Box 8409, Philadelphia, PA 19101-8409.
  • In person: the Municipal Services Building at 1401 John F. Kennedy Blvd. (cash accepted), plus satellite offices at 7522 Castor Ave. and 2761 N. 22nd St. that take no cash. Offices open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

The City's rate page lists 1.3998 percent for tax year 2025. For a house assessed at $200,000 with no exemption, that works out to a $2,799.60 bill.

What happens when a Philadelphia tax bill goes unpaid?

The account moves through a fixed ladder. Charges begin the day after the March 31 deadline and grow until the City treats the balance as delinquent and can move toward foreclosure.

  • From April 1: additions of 1.5 percent a month, running to January 1.
  • January 1: a further addition of up to 15 percent, a lien in the amount of the whole delinquency, and the account is registered delinquent.
  • February 1: penalties, attorney's fees and other costs are layered on, according to the Department's warning letter.
  • Any time after that: legal action, which can end in a sheriff sale of the house at public auction.

The Department sends a Warning of Risk of Tax Foreclosure to accounts with a balance and no payment agreement. Its text says a 2026 bill left unpaid by December 31, 2026, lets the City start foreclosure, and that debt from earlier years can be pursued at any time. The notice also points owners to free housing counseling and legal help through the City's housing agencies.

How does the Owner-occupied Payment Agreement work in Philadelphia?

The Owner-occupied Payment Agreement, or OOPA, lets a homeowner who lives in the house repay old tax in monthly amounts tied to income. An owner whose name is not on the deed can qualify if a legal interest in the home can be shown, and no down payment is needed. Some low-income and senior households pay $0 a month.

Tiers 4 and 5 fold new year taxes into the agreement. Everyone else must pay each new March 31 bill in full on top of the monthly plan amount. Applicants show two forms of proof of residence, one a government photo ID, and income records such as tax returns, pay stubs or benefit letters. A household of four earning $3,100 a month, for example, pays 8 percent, or $248, and has half the accrued interest waived. A review of actual expenses is available when the tiered amount is unaffordable.

Which other City charges can become liens on a Philadelphia house?

Property tax is not the only debt that can attach to the parcel. The Department's warning letter lists several others that the City can file as liens:

  • Water and sewer charges, with questions going to the Water Revenue Bureau at (215) 685-6300.
  • Commercial trash fees, previously called refuse fees.
  • Department of Licenses and Inspections abatement invoices.
  • Nuisance and demolition fees and fines.

Water liens can be searched at water-lien.phila.gov, which reports up to 15 years of recorded liens. The page says the results do not replace a title search and may omit court costs. If the search shows a lien, a payoff request form goes to the Water Department by email.

What does the Philadelphia housing market look like in Census data?

Philadelphia covers about 134 square miles, with a July 2025 population estimate of 1,574,281. William Penn's original plan covered only the area between Vine and South Streets and the Delaware and Schuylkill Rivers, and the old districts that the 1854 consolidation absorbed, such as Southwark and Kensington, survive as neighborhood names.

  • Typical owned home value: $243,100 for 2020 through 2024.
  • Share of households that own: 51.8 percent.
  • Median gross rent: $1,397 a month, with 679,428 households averaging 2.26 people.
  • Median household income: $61,953, and 21.4 percent of residents in poverty.
  • Mean commute: 31.7 minutes.

Interstates 76, 95 and 676 serve the city, and the county's highest point, 432 feet, sits in Chestnut Hill.

Which relief programs can Philadelphia homeowners apply for?

The City runs several programs that cut a bill or spread it out, and the Tax Center has a combined application that checks eligibility for five of them at once. Owners already enrolled generally do not reapply unless the property changes hands.

  • The Homestead Exemption takes $100,000 off the taxable assessment of an owner-occupied home in 2027, and the City says most owners save about $1,399.
  • The Real Estate Tax installment plan lets seniors and income-qualified owners pay the year in monthly installments instead of one lump sum.
  • The senior and low-income freezes hold the tax at its current level even if rates or values climb.
  • The Longtime Owner Occupants Program caps the taxable value for owners of ten or more years whose assessment jumped 50 percent in a year or 75 percent over five.
  • A credit applies to the City portion for reserve and National Guard members called to active duty.

Pennsylvania's own Property Tax/Rent Rebate program for seniors and adults with disabilities does not require a City tax receipt.

How can I sell a Philadelphia house when tax is due?

The tax debt does not block a sale. The closing figure simply has to cover what the City is owed.

  1. Look up the balance on the Philadelphia Tax Center by address or OPA number.
  2. Search water-lien.phila.gov and send a water payoff form at least 30 days before settlement.
  3. Ask a housing counselor about an OOPA first if you want to stay in the home.
  4. Order a title search to catch trash fee, abatement and other liens.
  5. Budget for the 4.578 percent realty transfer tax and the deed recording fee.

A seller on a short clock can ask for a cash offer, and the title company settles the City's claim at the table.

More questions about Philadelphia, PA Property Tax Guide

Who do I call about a Philadelphia property tax balance?

The Department of Revenue. You can check a balance on the Philadelphia Tax Center or call its customer service line. Its Warning of Risk of Tax Foreclosure letter also lists the Water Revenue Bureau at (215) 685-6300 for water charges.

What if I cannot pay my Philadelphia property tax in full?

Apply for a payment agreement. An owner who lives in the house can ask for an OOPA, and owners who do not live there can request a standard agreement. Income-based programs can lower or pause payments.

Can Philadelphia take my house for unpaid property tax?

Yes, after the account becomes delinquent and a lien is filed. The City can then seek a court order to sell the house at a sheriff sale. A signed payment agreement or full payment stops the process.

Do Philadelphia penalties start on March 31?

They start April 1. Additions of 1.5 percent a month accrue from that date until January 1, when the larger delinquency charges apply.

Does the buyer or seller pay the Philadelphia tax at closing?

The seller pays what is owed through closing out of the seller's side of the settlement statement. Both parties normally split the 4.578 percent transfer tax, though the City may collect it from either.

Which offices handle property tax in Pittsburgh?

Pittsburgh owners deal with three taxing bodies: the city, the school district and Allegheny County. The city's Real Estate Division handles billing and collection of the city tax, while the county sets the assessed value that every rate is applied to. The city's Real Estate Taxes page says the tax applies to all owners of real estate within the city and school district, calculated by multiplying the millage rate by the assessed value.

The city's Real Estate Division sits at 414 Grant Street and answers at 412-255-2525. The city first levied the tax in 1816, and Chapter 263 of the Pittsburgh Code covers it. Bills usually go out in the middle of January, with installment bills mailed in April and July.

The county's role is separate. The Allegheny County Office of Property Assessments decides what your house is worth for tax purposes, and the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review hears disputes. If your bill looks wrong, work out whether the problem is the value (a county matter) or the payment record (a city matter) before you call anyone.

When is Pittsburgh property tax due?

The year's bill can be paid in one amount or in three installments, and the dates repeat every year.

  • February 10: last day to take the 2 percent discount, on either the full annual amount or the first installment
  • February 27: first installment due, or the annual amount at its gross figure
  • April 30: second installment due
  • July 31: third installment due

The first installment is where people get caught. A payment that misses the end of February, or falls short of the whole first installment, makes the entire year's tax due, with interest running from March 1. An online payment portal run by Magic Collection Solutions is linked from the city page.

A taxpayer who misses the discount can ask for an extension using the discount extension form on the city's Real Estate Forms page.

How much is the tax rate in Pittsburgh?

Allegheny County's community profile for the city lists three millage rates for 2026: 6.43 mills for the county, 9.67 for the city and 10.457 for the school district. Added together that is 26.557 mills, or $2,655.70 a year on a property assessed at $100,000.

The same profile shows how that changed. In 2025 the city rate was 8.06 and the county rate was 6.43, so the total on $100,000 was $2,474.00. In 2024 the county rate was 4.73 and the total was $2,304.00. The profile puts the taxable residential median value at $68,600 and the 2026 total at $1,821.81 for a home at that value.

How does a Pittsburgh owner contest an assessment?

Disputes over value are heard by the Allegheny County Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review, which sits outside city government. Beginning with the 2027 annual season the board handles scheduling and hearing notices on its own.

The 2027 annual appeal window ran from July 1 to September 1, 2026, and it has closed. The county says a person who misses the window may file under limited circumstances, but first has to submit a late-filed appeal form. Check with the county before the next tax year's window opens.

  • Residential hearing notices are mailed at least 14 days ahead; commercial notices at least 21 days ahead.
  • The board meets every two weeks at 8:00 am in Room 328 of the County Office Building, 542 Forbes Avenue.
  • The 2027 common level ratio is 49.3 percent, and the county says it applies to current market value in appeals heard starting September 2026.

The common level ratio matters because an appeal compares the assessed value with market value after that factor is applied. Bring recent comparable sales and any repair estimates to the hearing.

What relief programs does Pittsburgh offer homeowners?

The city's property tax worksheet page lists two measures meant to lower a bill: the Act 50 homestead exemption of $15,000 and the Act 77 senior tax relief, described as a 40 percent reduction on assessment. The same page lists the city's millage as 9.67, matching the county profile above.

Eligibility rules, forms and filing dates come from the county and city offices, so ask the Real Estate Division or the Office of Property Assessments before you assume a reduction applies to your parcel.

What happens if a Pittsburgh house is sold with back taxes?

Old delinquent taxes are split between two collectors. The city keeps prior-year delinquent City, Library and Parks real estate taxes and answers questions at 412-255-2525. Prior-year delinquent school taxes were turned over to Jordan Tax Service, Inc., which takes payment arrangements at 412-345-7960.

Anyone can download the city's delinquency list. It warns that the list may not show the current owner if the county has not yet reported a transfer, may not reflect assessment changes decided on appeal, and may leave out accounts under $50. In practice that means a title search is the safer check, and the payoff figure should come directly from the city and the collection agency in writing.

At settlement, the agent subtracts unpaid taxes from what the seller receives and sends the money to the collectors. If the debts exceed the price, the settlement statement shows the shortfall before anyone signs.

What does the transfer tax cost on a Pittsburgh sale?

Allegheny County says its realty transfer tax runs from 2 to 5 percent, and Pittsburgh sits at the top of that range. The county's worked example for a house in the city shows 5 percent in total: 1 percent to the state, 3 percent to the city and 1 percent to the Pittsburgh School District. On a $40,000 sale that is $2,000. County pages say the city applied the 5 percent rate to residential deeds recorded starting February 1, 2020.

Payment happens at recording, on its own check apart from the recording fees. State rules hold both sides liable, and certain transfers, such as inheritances, are exempt. The sale contract decides who actually pays.

What is Pittsburgh like for owners and sellers?

The city covers about 55 square miles in the center of Allegheny County, with steep slopes, rolling hills and floodplains along the Allegheny, Monongahela and Ohio rivers. The county's profile divides it into 32 wards, from Squirrel Hill and Shadyside to Lawrenceville, Brookline, Carrick and the North Side. Slope and floodplain exposure differ a great deal from one neighborhood to the next.

  • Headcount in mid 2025: 307,632, which is 1.5 percent above the 2020 base
  • Owners occupy 47.7 percent of occupied homes
  • An owned home typically carries a $205,800 value
  • Gross rent in the middle runs $1,261
  • 138,188 households, averaging 2.03 people
  • Household income in the middle: $65,742

All of these are from Census QuickFacts for Pittsburgh, on its 2020 to 2024 survey basis. With fewer than half of occupied homes owner-occupied, renters make up the majority of Pittsburgh households.

More questions about Pittsburgh, PA Property Tax Guide

What is the Pittsburgh discount deadline?

February 10. Paying the full annual tax or the first installment by that date earns a 2 percent discount. After that, the gross amount is due February 27.

What happens if I skip the first installment?

You owe the whole year at once, and interest starts March 1. The same result follows from paying less than the full first installment.

Where can I get answers on a Pittsburgh tax bill?

Call the city's Real Estate Division at 412-255-2525 or visit 414 Grant Street. Questions about the value itself belong with the Allegheny County Office of Property Assessments.

Can I appeal my Pittsburgh assessment now?

The 2027 annual appeal window ran July 1 to September 1, 2026, and has closed. A late-filed appeal form is available under limited circumstances. Ask the county for the next window.

Who gets paid when a house with back taxes sells?

The title company pays them from the seller's proceeds. Delinquent city taxes go to the city's finance department, and prior-year school taxes go to Jordan Tax Service, Inc. Get written payoff figures first.
